report:
# Research Summary: Hands-Only CPR and Survival After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest

**Conclusion: The claim is well-supported by evidence.** Bystander hands-only (compression-only) CPR is associated with greater survival than no bystander CPR, and it performs comparably to conventional CPR with rescue breathing in adults.

## Evidence

**Compression-only CPR vs. no CPR:** A meta-analysis in *Circulation* found that dispatcher-assisted chest-compression-only bystander CPR was associated with improved survival compared to standard CPR, and both types of bystander CPR clearly outperform no CPR at all ([PMC2987687](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2987687/)). This aligns with the American Heart Association's 2008 Science Advisory, which concluded that adult victims receiving either hands-only or conventional bystander CPR have similar—and better—survival chances than those receiving no CPR ([ahajournals.org](https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/circulationaha.107.189380)).

**Bystander CPR (any type) vs. no CPR:** A study on 30-day survival found bystander CPR was associated with higher survival among adults with presumed non-cardiac cause OHCA, and survival rates improved over the study period as bystander CPR rates rose ([PubMed 31129226](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31129226/)). Additional adjusted-analysis research confirms both compression-only and conventional bystander CPR were associated with higher survival compared to no bystander CPR ([PMC9803815](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9803815/)).

**Important nuance—compression-only vs. conventional CPR:** While hands-only CPR beats no CPR, evidence is mixed on whether it's superior to conventional CPR with breaths. A 2021 meta-analysis found no significant differences between compression-only and standard CPR outcomes ([PubMed 34622436](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34622436/)), and pediatric-specific studies suggest conventional CPR may be advantageous for children specifically.

## Bottom Line
Your claim is accurate for adults: hands-only CPR clearly improves survival versus no bystander action. The debate in current literature centers on whether hands-only is *better than* conventional CPR—not whether it helps compared to doing nothing.
